abstract: The use of technology-based learning systems to provide individualized instruction through tutoring for K-12 students is gaining increased attention. We discuss the development of pedagogical components of Personalized Learning2 (PL2), a human mentoring online system that supports both mentors and students while improving student's math achievement. PL2 uses AI-driven software to recommend custom resources and supports based on mentor input and student math learning data. This research focuses on developing a more efficient and research-based method of resource organization by creating a schema of mentoring competencies. The survey results ranked mentor skills according to the perceptions of partner members, demonstrating Engage and Motivate Students as the most important skill. These results guided the creation of a preliminary super-competency scheme through SMART supports (Social-emotional, Math Content, Advocacy, Relationships, Technology).
shortDescription: AI-driven online mentoring system enhances K-12 math achievement through customized resources and mentor training.

title: Supporting Mentoring and Math Instruction with AI Software
venue: Pennsylvania Statewide STEM Ecosystem Working Group

title: Student-Teacher Relationships Drive Student Help-Seeking for Math Learning
Perceptions of Preparedness and Success Inform Undergraduates' Feelings of Belonging
A narrative inquiry of critical moments in students' paths to math success
abstract: Students' individual experiences can contribute to a richer understanding of the personal and environmental barriers students experience in learning math. We conducted a narrative inquiry study of six focus groups in which students discussed their challenges in learning math, as well as the resources and strategies that helped them overcome barriers. Results suggest that narratives can raise new areas for investigating learning processes and practical suggestions for better supporting math learners.
shortDescription: Students' personal experiences and family environments significantly impact their math learning.

title: Computer-supported human mentoring for personalized and equitable math learning
abstract: Computer tutor data indicate that more learning opportunities yield greater achievement, but also confirm there are gaps in the number and quality of opportunities marginalized students receive that technology alone does not address. Personalized learning with mentors can close this gap in opportunities but is expensive to implement. We introduce a free, web-based application, Personalized Learning2 (PL2), designed to improve mentoring efficiency by connecting mentors to intervention and instructional resources. Preliminary findings indicated that PL2's categorization of students based on math learning software data enabled mentors to focus their efforts, and that mentors found PL2 resources to positively expand how they taught and mentored.
shortDescription: PL2 is a free web app that enhances mentoring efficiency and helps close opportunity gaps for marginalized students.

title: Interactions with peers on the path to math success
abstract: A key strategy to being successful in math is help-seeking. Much research has focused on how students seek help from teachers, but students also benefit from peer assistance. We analyzed conversations from eight focus groups related to students' paths to success in math. We found that students frequently brought up peer interactions as critical to their success. Three emergent themes were: support versus comparison, balance of effort within study groups, and friends versus peers. Our findings have implications for classroom and group structures, including encouraging peer help-seeking and help-giving, as well as addressing belonging and sense of community.
shortDescription: Peer interactions are crucial for math success, highlighting the need to encourage peer help-seeking in classrooms.

title: Building strategies for a personalized learning mentor app: A design case
Comprehensive views of math learners: A case for modeling non-math factors in adaptive software
abstract: Adaptive math software supports students' learning by targeting specific math knowledge components. However, widespread use of adaptive math software in classrooms has not led to the expected changes in student achievement, particularly for racially minoritized students and students situated in poverty. While research has shown the power of human mentors to support student learning and reduce opportunity gaps, mentoring support could be optimized by using educational technology to identify the specific non-math factors that are disrupting students' learning. In this paper, we present an analysis of one non-math factor - reading comprehension - that has been shown to influence math learning. We predict math performance using this non-math factor and show that it contributes novel explanatory value in modeling students' learning behaviors.
shortDescription: Integrating educational technology to address non-math factors like reading comprehension can enhance mentoring support.

title: Dosage and Dialogue: What Drives Student Math Progress in One-on-One Human-AI Hybrid Tutoring?
abstract: One-on-one human tutoring is among the most effective educational interventions, yet cost and staffing constraints limit scalability. Hybrid human-AI tutoring, in which students work in math learning software while receiving as-needed one-on-one (1:1) support from a remote human tutor, offers a promising alternative-but its effectiveness, and the role of how much and how well tutoring is delivered, remain under-characterized. Drawing on a technology-enhanced learning perspective, we test competing predictions about how human tutoring dosage and instructional quality combine to shape learning: (i) a complementarity hypothesis in which higher-quality human tutoring amplifies the effectiveness of human tutoring dosage, and (ii) a threshold hypothesis in which only sustained, "instructional" interactions matter. We analyze tutoring and platform log data from two U.S. middle-school implementations of hybrid math tutoring (IXL: N=203; MATHia: N=157), linked to end-of-year external assessments. Dosage is operationalized as cumulative human tutor-student minutes and counts of 1:1 sessions, filtered to exclude brief check-ins (<1 minute). For the transcript-available site, we include a validated LLM-derived tutoring rating computed from full-session dialogues using a rubric/codebook. Regression models show that more frequent sustained tutoring sessions are associated with greater in-platform math progress after controlling for prior achievement. In contexts with transcript data, LLM-derived tutoring rating further explains variation beyond human tutoring dosage. In contrast, direct associations between raw dosage and external test scores are weaker and context-dependent, while in-platform progress is consistently predictive of external performance.
